To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 3 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: alpha_level

power_id power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
1 apriori other 24 NA 0.80 0.264 Cohen’s f G*Power
2 apriori other 28 NA 0.90 0.264 Cohen’s f G*Power
3 apriori other 32 NA 0.95 0.264 Cohen’s f G*Power
power_id text
1;2;3 The original authors reported a partial eta-squared effect size of 0.07 for their key analysis of interest, the Condition x Block interaction. This roughly translates to a partial Cohen’s f of 0.87. Looking at the non-partial effect sizes, they are an etasquared of about 0.066 and Cohen’s f of about 0.264, indicating a medium effect size. Thus, a power analysis to detect an interaction with a medium effect size in a mixed ANOVA was conducted using G*Power (Faul et al., 2009). The power analysis indicated that a sample of 24 participants was needed to achieve 80% power, 28 participants were needed to achieve 90% power, and 32 participants were needed to achieve 95% power. However, we decided to match the original study’s sample size in order to replicate it as closely as possible. We also thought this would allow for the detection of smaller effects, as we anticipated may be the case since we were running the study online rather than in the lab.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 4 imprecise p values out of 13 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

What we found

All effect sizes were reported, but some appear inconsistent with the test statistic. This can be because the effect size is not clearly labeled (e.g., d, instead of d_rm), because the effect sizes is not reported with enough precisions (e.g., 0.3 instead of 0.32), or because the effect size is incorrectly reported.

Show details

All tests had effect sizes, but some effect sizes do not match the reported test statistic.

For t-tests with a reported d, coherence checks yielded 11 matches under assumptions, 1 no match.

For F-tests with a reported eta-squared effect size, coherence checks yielded 14 matches under assumptions, 2 no matches.

For metascientific articles demonstrating that effect sizes are often not reported:

  • Peng, C.-Y. J., Chen, L.-T., Chiang, H.-M., & Chiang, Y.-C. (2013). The Impact of APA and AERA Guidelines on Effect Size Reporting. Educational Psychology Review, 25(2), 157–209. doi:[10.1007/s10648-013-9218-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-013-9218-2).

For educational material on reporting effect sizes:

  • Guide to Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 16 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 5053 of 13929 data columns (36%) are documented in a codebook; 8876 are not.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 4 codebook/README/label sources and 13929 data columns across 353 files.

To check (5)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 5 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = 1.00 The key analysis of interest was a mixed ANOVA with Condition as a betweensubjects factor and Block as a within-subjects factor, from which the original paper reported a significant Condition x Block interaction, F(24,568) = 1.66, p < .01, ηp² = 0.07, 95% CI [0.00, 0.07], and main effect of Condition, F(3, 71) = 3.18, p < .03, ηp² = 0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.25]. 1 In the replication data, there was not a significant Condition x Block interaction, F(24, 648) = 0.235, p = 1.00, ηpfoot_1 = 0.009 2, but there was a main effect of Condition, F(3, 648) = 6.774, p < .001, ηp² = 0.03, 95% CI [0.01, 0.06].
p = .474 In the replication, the Auditory Label and Written Label conditions were significantly different from each other, t(648) = 4.247, p < .0001, Cohen’s d = 0.459, 95% CI [0.25, 0.67], and the Location and No Label conditions were not, t(648) = -1.094, p = .474, Cohen’s d = -0.118, 95% CI [-0.33, 0.09].
p = .990 In the ANOVA with the pooled data, there was not a significant Condition x Block interaction, F(8, 666) = 0.205, p = .990, ηp² = 0.002 2, with the effect being smaller than the lower bound of the original effect’s confidence interval.
p = .974 In the replication data, the interaction was not significant, F(8, 324) = 0.276, p = .974, ηp² = 0.007, 95% CI [0.00, 0.0004]foot_2 .
p = .339 They also found that an ANOVA with Condition as a between-subjects factor was significant, which was not the case in our replication data, F(2, 54) = 1.105, p = .339, ηp² = 0.04, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16].

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Study/Repository Mismatch

The studies named in the manuscript do not match how the repository’s files are grouped: the manuscript names studies (ex1, ex2) with no matching files in the repository; the repository separates out a study (pilot1) not named in the manuscript. Check that every study has its own clearly-named folder or file prefix, and that the folder names match how the manuscript refers to each study.

File Naming

File names should be machine-parseable: no spaces or special characters, and every file should be classifiable by name or extension. We found 3 naming problems that should be fixed, and 180 files with a naming suggestion (not required, but a good habit).

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 7 distinct packages/libraries: codebookr, effectsize, emmeans, lme4, lmerTest, patchwork, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 353 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

To check Reproducibility Check

  • We assessed 4 R code files for reproducibility and ran them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 5 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
  • 3 of 4 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 1 did not finish within the time limit.
  • 7 installable dependencies detected.
  • 1006 statistics stored from the extracted output; 25 of 59 reported tests matched (42.4%).

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 4 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. 5 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

3 of 4 scripts ran to the end: 1 did not finish within our time limit.

Script Result What happened
final_analyses_revisions.R Ran out of time It was still running after 300 seconds, our time limit per script.
final_analyses.R Ran to the end
get_original_CIs.R Ran to the end
Replication Report.qmd Ran to the end

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • final_analyses_revisions.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 59 statistical tests reported in the paper, 25 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 4 R code files.

Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, source() call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 final_analyses_revisions.R — none
2 final_analyses.R — none
3 get_original_CIs.R — none
4 Replication Report.qmd — none

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 3 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

> clean_data = function(dat, index) {
>   dat_clean <- dat %>% 
>     mutate(participant = index) %>% 
>     mutate(counterbalance_group = counterbalance_group[1]) %>% 
>     select(participant,
>            age,
>            gender,
>            counterbalance_group,
>            exp_name,
>            block,
>            alien_stim,
>            category,
>            friendly,
>            approach,
>            key_resp_actual,
>            correct,
>            trial_started,
>            trial_stopped) %>% 
>     drop_na(alien_stim) %>% 
>     mutate(trial = 1:144) %>%
>     filter(trial_stopped - trial_started <= 180) %>% #remove trial if more than 3 minutes long
>     mutate(condition = filter(condition_names,
>                               dat$exp_name[1] == experimentName)$condition) %>% 
>     mutate(gender = case_when(
>       gender == "male" ~ "M",
>       gender == "MALE" ~ "M",
>       gender == "Male" ~ "M",
>       gender == "make" ~ "M", #assuming this was a typo someone had
>       gender == "Female" ~"F",
>       gender == "female" ~ "F"
>     )) %>% 
>     mutate(age = ifelse(test = age == 7, #someone put their age as 7, assuming this is a fluke since you must be over 18 to be on Prolific
>                         yes = NA,
>                         no = age))
>   
>   return (dat_clean)
> }
> get_verification_scores = function(dat, index) {
>   verification_score <- dat %>% 
>     mutate(condition = filter(condition_names,
>                               dat$exp_name[1] == experimentName)$condition) %>% 
>     filter(!is.na(verification_correct)) %>% 
>     select(condition, verification_correct) %>% 
>     mutate(participant = index) %>% 
>     group_by(participant, condition) %>% 
>     summarize(verification_sum = sum(verification_correct))
>   return (verification_score)
> }
> check_responses = function(dat) {
>   if (nrow(filter(dat, key_resp_actual == "[\"up\"]"))/144 > 0.9|
>       nrow(filter(dat, key_resp_actual == "[\"down\"]"))/144 > 0.9|
>       nrow(filter(dat, key_resp_actual == "[\"right\"]"))/144 > 0.9|
>       nrow(filter(dat, key_resp_actual == "[\"left\"]"))/144 > 0.9) {
>     return (FALSE)
>   } else {
>     return (TRUE)
>   }
> }

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

5 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: Replication Report Pre-registration.qmd at https://osf.io/download/egz52/?view_only=0a18126d16e84cc8b26320fb0ac422d3 (same as Replication Report.qmd at https://osf.io/download/mahnf/); Replication Report Pre-registration.qmd at https://osf.io/download/egz52/ (same as Replication Report.qmd at https://osf.io/download/mahnf/); final_analyses.R at https://osf.io/download/b6c9z/ (same as final_analyses.R at https://osf.io/download/b6c9z/?view_only=0a18126d16e84cc8b26320fb0ac422d3); get_original_CIs.R at https://osf.io/download/qy9pv/ (same as get_original_CIs.R at https://osf.io/download/qy9pv/?view_only=0a18126d16e84cc8b26320fb0ac422d3); final_analyses_revisions.R at https://osf.io/download/xqv5j/ (same as final_analyses_revisions.R at https://osf.io/download/xqv5j/?view_only=0a18126d16e84cc8b26320fb0ac422d3).

Reported vs. reproduced

59 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 25 matched (19 fully, 6 partially) — 42.4% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

In Experiment 2 of the study, the authors compared four conditions of the category learning task, Auditory Label, Written Label, Location, and No Label, while in Experiment 1 only Written Label and No Label conditions were used.In the Auditory Label and Written Label conditions, participants were given the nonsense words “leebish” and “grecious” as labels for the two alien categories.

Twenty-one participants completed the task, 11 in the Label condition and 10 in the No Label condition.

  1. Methods Participants 76 participants completed the study, ages 22-78 (M = 44).

Nineteen participants were randomly assigned to each of the four conditions.

Participants were recruited online through Prolific and compensated $8/hr.

Participants were required to be fluent in English, to ensure they would understand the instructions of the task.

In the task, participants were tasked with learning two groups of aliens.

In the instructions, participants were told that if they believe the alien should be approached, they should press the arrow key on their keyboard that would result in the astronaut moving toward the alien.

Participants completed 9 blocks of 16 trials of the category learning trials, which is the same length as the original study.

No verification trials were given in the No Label condition, as their purpose was to measure how well participants were learning the association between the alien stimuli and cues (labels or locations).

The power analysis indicated that a sample of 24 participants was needed to achieve 80% power, 28 participants were needed to achieve 90% power, and 32 participants were needed to achieve 95% power.

This is because the differences in the tasks across studies are minor, as participants completed the task at a computer in the original study as well (just inperson rather than online).

With our participant sample, we are not able to subsample to the original study age range, as only 3 participants fall in the range of 18-24.

Additionally, since the original study participants were all college students, this could be another relevant difference that would remain even if age was equated.

We do not have this information from our participants, and the original study did not report this information.

Ethics approval statement:

Caroline Kaicher: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Project administration, Resources, Software, Supervision, Validation, Visualization, Writing -original draft, Writing -review & editing • Ellen M. Markman: Conceptualization, Writing -review & editing • Laura Gwilliams: Conceptualization, Writing -review & editing Ethical Statement This research was approved by the IRB of Stanford University under protocol #IRB-23274.

The procedures used in this study adhere to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki.
