(4) Evaluation

Even though the replication data show a partial replication of the primary analysis of interest (the main effect of Condition), the lack of a Condition x Block interaction fails to support the main claim made in the original paper: adults learn categories quicker if they have labels versus when they do not. While the Auditory Label group performed better than the No Label group, the Written Label group had lower performance than the Auditory Label and Location groups. This suggests that having a label is not always beneficial in this category learning task. Lastly, while performance on the verification trials was numerically higher for the Auditory Label group compared to the Written Label and Location groups, this was not a statistically significant difference. The benefit of having a label may be sensitive to task implementation and participant population differences.

4.1 Feedback from the original study's authors

Comment provided by Gary Lupyan:

We commend the authors for undertaking this replication of our 2007 study and thank the authors for providing this opportunity to comment. Our original study has been the subject of numerous extensions, as we review below. However, to our knowledge there have not been prior exact replications. The closest is Lupyan and Casasanto (2015) who successfully replicated the main effect of labels (though with slightly different stimuli), and Brojde et al., (2011) who showed that labels significantly interfere with category learning when the category contrast is not based on shape (see also Tolins & Colunga, 2013; and Mertens et al., 2025 for a partial replication). When it is based on shape (as in the original study), labels were found to lead to numerically, but not significantly better learning. Other work aiming to investigate effects of labels on learning different types of categories, found labels to help learning of probabilistic categories (Fotiadis & Protopapas, 2014) as well as learning hard-to-name shape-based categories in a within-subject design (Fotiadis & Protopapas, 2023). The facilitating effect of labels has also been extended to other modalities, e.g., in learning olfactory (Vanek et al., 2021) and tactile (Miller et al., 2018) categories. An attempt to find effects of labels on emotion-categories was unsuccessful (Hoemann et al., 2022). Consistent with our proposal that labels affect category learning by highlighting category-diagnostic features (e.g., Lupyan, 2012), a number of findings have confirmed that labels selectively increase looking toward diagnostic features in both children and adults (Althaus & Mareschal, 2014; Barnhart et al., 2018).

One factor that may help explain the present non-replication is the lower overall categorization accuracy observed here compared to the original experiments. It is possible that online testing may have contributed to a lower general engagement with the task, contributing to a larger proportion of participants (in both conditions) who struggled with the basic task. It is also worth noting that the sample sizes in the original sizes were small by current standards; we cannot rule out that the original effect size was therefore an over-estimate. We hope this replication attempt, together with the broader literature, will help the field develop a clearer picture of the conditions under which labels facilitate category learning and home in on the factors that modulate this effect.

4.2 Limitations and Recommendations for Future Replications

The major difference between this replication study and the original study is that the replication was done online and the original was in-person. It is possible that this influenced the findings, especially given that the participants' overall performance was lower than the original study.

Some work has suggested that switching to online for a replication study when the original was done in person, compared to using the same modality for both the original and replication, results in lower replicability (Boyce et al., 2023). We speculate that this may be for a couple of reasons: 1) conducting a study online introduces more flexibility for participants in the amount of attention paid to the task, meaning that the participants may not be reliably engaged throughout the task, or 2) it could be due to the differences introduced to the task when converting it to an online task. In our case, any validity concerns would most likely coincide with the first possibility. This is because the differences in the tasks across studies are minor, as participants completed the task at a computer in the original study as well (just inperson rather than online). Technical differences include uncontrolled screen size, visual angle, and audio delivery (e.g., volume, headphone vs speakers), as well as potential noise introduced to the stimulus presentation timing as a result of using browser-based timing. These differences can be reduced in future replications through additional checks such as standardized audio checks and timing validation procedures.

Ideally, the effect would be robust enough to survive potential differences in level of participant engagement -however, it is difficult to know whether the nonreplication of the primary analysis of interest, the Condition x Block interaction showing a benefit of having labels, was due to this difference. The present study does not include attention checks, which would be helpful in determining how the level of participant engagement affected the results (Cuskley & Sulik, 2024). Additionally, in the present study there are wide confidence intervals for some effects, especially in the exploratory analyses using the mixed effects model. This indicates that some estimated effects are not precise. It is also worth noting, as the original author does above, that the original study may have overestimated the size of the effect. In addition, our inferred confidence intervals from the original study include 0 for both the Condition x Block interaction and main effect of Condition. In light of these considerations, we suggest that future attempts to replicate this effect should aim to detect smaller effect sizes and include more participants. Additionally, we recommend including attention checks to ensure sufficient data quality.

Another difference between this study and the original study is the age range of participants. Our study had participants with ages ranging from 22-78, while the original study had college student participants ranging from ages 18-24. The greater age range in our replication may have introduced more variation that resulted in our smaller effect size. Our exploratory analyses showed that age did not substantially influence our main analysis of interest, the Condition x Block interaction. However, we did see that for the younger half of participants, the difference in performance on the Auditory Label and No Label conditions was much greater than in our full sample. This could perhaps be due to a higher prevalence of hearing loss in older adults, thus hindering their performance in the Auditory Label condition (Agrawal et al., 2008).

With our participant sample, we are not able to subsample to the original study age range, as only 3 participants fall in the range of 18-24. Additionally, since the original study participants were all college students, this could be another relevant difference that would remain even if age was equated. Therefore, while it seems that age in general did not influence our ability to detect the main analysis of interest, it is not possible to know whether the effect would have been replicated if the participant samples were more closely matched on age and other demographics such as education status. Additionally, while both samples were English speakers, another potential difference between samples could be first language and language(s) spoken, which are relevant to language processing. We do not have this information from our participants, and the original study did not report this information.

As detailed above, there are a number of demographic differences between participant samples in the original study and our replication. Future work could help gain further clarity as to what extent these differences influence the label benefit in category learning, and inform how researchers can investigate this phenomenon in children.

4.3 Brief Evaluation

□ success X failure □ mixed □ inconclusive

(5) Social Impact & Responsibility

Fine-grained category knowledge is often acquired with the help of linguistic labels in adults, and is a form of expertise across many domains. While this project aimed to replicate the finding that linguistic labels boost fine-grained category learning for adults, this was intended as a first step before extending the experimental paradigm to children. Examining the development of this ability in children helps us understand how surprisingly sophisticated world knowledge can develop at a young age. Additionally, the broader goal of understanding the mechanisms supporting category learning in children can be translated to the educational context in the form of pedagogical applications.
